claims.text: Demographic parity best matches the fairness choices made by the majority of individuals in group fairness scenarios.
Explanations for decisions made by algorithmic decision-making systems increase user perceptions of fairness in news recommender systems.
Conservative users perceive the inclusion of sensitive features like gender and race in algorithmic decision-making systems as fairer than liberal users do.
Individuals tend to perceive algorithms as fairer when the algorithmic decision yields a outcome that directly benefits them.
Perceived fairness of algorithms has a significant positive impact on satisfaction with algorithmic systems.

evidence.description: Srivastava et al. (2019) matched participant fairness choices with group fairness definitions across criminal and skin cancer risk scenarios, showing demographic parity best matched participant choices.
Shin (2021) demonstrated that decision explanations in AI-based news recommender systems significantly increased respondents' perceptions of fairness.
Grgić-Hlača et al. (2020; 2018) found conservative users evaluated the inclusion of sensitive features such as race and gender in ADM as fairer compared to liberal users.
Grgić-Hlača et al. (2020) and R. Wang et al. (2020) observed that self-interest influences perceptions, making outcomes that personally benefit users seem fairer.
Shin and Park (2019) found that perceived fairness positively impacts user satisfaction with algorithms to a degree exceeding perceived transparency.

methodologies.name: Systematic Literature Review
methodologies.description: Synthesized empirical research on fairness perceptions of algorithmic decision-making across 39 empirical studies using PICOC and PRISMA framework guidelines.
conditions: Two-stage screening process with inter-rater reliability calculation (Cohen's Kappa)

limitations.text: The review cannot make assertions about studies on perceived algorithmic fairness published in languages other than English due to the choice of search strings and databases.
Data on citizens' perceptions of algorithmic fairness in existing empirical literature is almost exclusively collected in Western-democratic contexts.
The existing empirical literature lacks a coherent, multi-dimensional theoretical concept and validated measurement scale for perceived algorithmic fairness.

future_work.text: Diversify study populations by investigating fairness perceptions in non-Western contexts where ADM systems are widely implemented.
Develop and validate multi-dimensional measurement scales specifically designed for measuring fairness perceptions of ADM systems.
Adopt a society-in-the-loop framework to examine broader institutional implementations and trade-offs in algorithmic decision-making.
